name: Agent Skills
question: How do I give an agent many procedures without flooding its context?
summary: A skill is a folder with instructions, scripts and reference files for one kind of task. Only each skill’s name and short description sit in the agent’s context; the full instructions load when a task matches, and bundled scripts run as code rather than being re-derived by the model. This progressive disclosure lets one agent carry dozens of procedures cheaply. Skills are code: review them, version them, and never install one you have not read.
useCases: Operations agents with many written procedures
Deterministic steps worth a script, such as date calculations or file checks

items.detail: specific enough that the agent picks the right one
body and files load only when relevant
forms, policies and examples read on demand
skills change behaviour like code does
third-party skills can carry harmful instructions

steps: Write one skill per procedure: a folder with SKILL.md, scripts and references
Make the description say what it does and when to use it
Move deterministic steps into scripts the skill runs
Review, version and test skills; read any third-party skill before installing
pitfalls: Vague descriptions, so the wrong skill loads
Pasting every procedure into the system prompt instead
Installing a downloaded skill without reading it
remember: Describe it well, load it late, script the exact parts.
caption: Illustrative: Paisapath, a fictional fintech, runs 30 operations procedures through one agent.

code.text: description: Respond to a card chargeback or disputed card charge,
including the response deadline, evidence list and customer message.
Use when a customer disputes a card transaction.
1. Run scripts/deadline.py with the dispute date and card network
to get the response deadline. Never compute dates yourself.
2. Collect evidence: order record, delivery proof, customer messages.
See reference/evidence.md for what each reason code needs.
4. If the amount is above ₹25,000, stop and hand over to a person.

steps.title: Name and describe it precisely
steps.text: The name and description are all the agent sees up front. “Respond to a card chargeback … Use when a customer disputes a card transaction” tells it exactly when to load this skill.

steps.title: Load the body only when needed
steps.text: Thirty descriptions cost about 3,000 tokens. The full instructions of this skill load only for chargeback tasks.

steps.title: Script the exact parts
steps.text: Deadlines depend on the card network and dates. A script computes them; the model never does date arithmetic in its head.

steps.title: Point to reference files
steps.text: Evidence rules per reason code live in a separate file, read only when the task gets that far.

steps.title: Put limits in the skill
steps.text: Amounts above ₹25,000 go to a person. The skill carries the policy, not just the steps.

steps.title: Review and version skills
steps.text: Skills change the agent’s behaviour, so they go through review like code. A downloaded skill is read before it is installed.

pros: Dozens of procedures for the context cost of their descriptions
Deterministic steps run as scripts, not model guesses
Procedures are files you can review, version and share
The same skill works across tasks and agents
cons: Scripts need an environment that can run them
Skills can carry harmful instructions if unreviewed
avoidWhen: A handful of short rules that fit comfortably in the system prompt
Actions that need a live API call (make it a tool)

practice.scenario: Paisapath, a fictional fintech, runs 30 operations procedures through one agent: KYC re-checks, chargebacks, GST invoice fixes and more. Each is a skill folder with a SKILL.md, scripts and reference files. Only the 30 names and descriptions sit in context; the chargeback skill's instructions and its deadline script load only when a customer disputes a charge. Every skill is reviewed and versioned like code.

industries.use: Chargebacks, KYC re-checks and refunds as reusable procedures
Claims intake checklists and document requirements per product
Release, migration and incident runbooks for coding agents

practice.analogy: A binder of standard operating procedures with a clear index: staff read the index every day, and open a procedure only when its case comes up.

numericDrill.question: Procedures in the system prompt add 45,000 tokens to every task; as skills they add 3,000 up front plus 2,000 when one loads. Over 1,000 tasks, how many tokens do skills save, in lakh?
numericDrill.answer: Prompt: 45,000 × 1,000 = 4.5 crore tokens. Skills: 5,000 × 1,000 = 50 lakh. Saving: 4 crore = 400 lakh tokens.

interview.question: What is an Agent Skill and why use one?
interview.answer: A folder with a SKILL.md, scripts and references for one task. Only its name and description sit in context; the body loads when a task matches. Many procedures fit in little context, and exact steps run as scripts.

interview.question: How do you keep skills safe?
interview.answer: Treat them as code: review, version and test them; read any third-party skill before installing; keep dangerous actions behind tools with policy checks.

mistakes.fix: Say what it does and when to use it

quiz.question: What does an agent see of a skill before it is needed?
quiz.explanation: Progressive disclosure keeps only metadata in context.

quiz.question: Where should an exact date calculation in a skill live?
options: In the instructions for the model to work out
In a bundled script the skill runs

quiz.question: Which description selects best?
options: "Respond to card chargebacks with deadline and evidence; use when a customer disputes a card charge"
quiz.explanation: Say what it does and when to use it.

quiz.question: Which belong in a skill folder? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Secrets never belong in a skill.

options: Read and review it before installing

quiz.question: When is a tool better than a skill?
options: When the action needs a live API call with typed inputs
quiz.explanation: Skills describe how; tools do the call.

quiz.question: Two skills have near-identical descriptions. What happens?
options: The agent may load the wrong one

quiz.question: How should skills be managed? Select all that apply.
options: Edited live in production without review
quiz.explanation: Skills change behaviour like code does.

quiz.question: At ₹0.25 per 1,000 tokens, what does 45,000 tokens per task cost for 1,000 tasks?
What is progressive disclosure?
options: Loading details only when they become relevant

quiz.question: A skill says "amounts above ₹25,000 go to a person". Why put it in the skill?
options: The limit travels with the procedure wherever it is used
It is required by the SDK

quiz.question: Right procedure is chosen 70% of the time with vague descriptions and 93% with specific ones. Out of 1,000 tasks, how many more are right?
Where are Claude Code project skills usually stored?
options: In the repository, reviewed like code

quiz.question: How does a skill relate to procedural memory?
options: Skills are written by people; procedural memory is procedures the agent learns and saves
Procedural memory is for tools only
quiz.explanation: Both store procedures; the author differs.

quiz.question: Which are risks with skills? Select all that apply.
options: Stale procedures after a policy change
Vague descriptions picking the wrong skill

quiz.question: Scripts in a skill need what at runtime?
options: An environment that can run code
quiz.explanation: Skills with scripts need code execution.

quiz.question: One skill body is 2,000 tokens and loads for 30% of tasks. Average added tokens per task?
Why not put all 30 procedures as tools?
options: Their schemas still cost context and tools suit actions more than long procedures
quiz.explanation: Tools are for actions; skills carry procedures.

quiz.question: What should a SKILL.md start with?
quiz.explanation: The metadata is what selection uses.
